title: Trailer unload & staging
instructions:
Phase: Arrival & Setup | Skill level: SOLO after training | Status: DRAFT
WHAT IT IS: Unloading the trailer and staging the day's equipment where it will be used. First-out gear comes off first so grinding can start without digging.
YOU NEED: Work gloves [SAFETY]; hand truck/dolly if carried [FLOOR]; the job load list (Trailer Checks tab)
SET UP: 1. Trailer reversed onto the driveway / work area, opened up.
Check the load list before touching anything — you unload to the list, not by memory.
DO THE WORK: 1. Unload in this order: extension cords, hand grinders, vacuums, then red grinder and generator.
Stage gear at the front of the trailer / near the work area — red grinder, vacuums, generator reachable first.
Keep walk paths clear — nothing in doorways or on stairs.
Resin kits stay upright, in shade, lids on, until the mixing station is set.
DONE LOOKS LIKE: Everything on the load list is off the trailer and staged where the lead wants it. Trailer doors can close. Nothing blocking the client's doors or driveway.
SAFETY: Gloves when handling grinders and kits. Two hands / two people for the red grinder ramp — never muscle it alone. Watch footing on ramps and wet driveways.
COMMON MISTAKES: Unloading everything 'just in case' (site becomes a pile, reload takes forever); kits left in direct sun; gear staged in the client's walkway.
STOP AND ASK: Anything on the load list is missing from the trailer — tell the lead BEFORE work starts, not when it's needed.
REPORT BACK: Lead: 'Unload done, everything on the list is here' — or name what's missing.

title: Power setup — 2 circuits / generator
instructions:
Phase: Arrival & Setup | Skill level: ASSIST+ | Status: DRAFT
WHAT IT IS: Getting safe, working power to grinders and vacuums. Grinder and vacuum must run on SEPARATE circuits or the breaker trips all day.
YOU NEED: Extension cords by length [VAC-POWER]; power splitter/adapters [VAC-POWER]; generator [FLOOR-FRONT]; fuel if generator day [per lead]
SET UP: 1. Ask the lead: house power or generator today?
If house: find 2 outlets on DIFFERENT breakers (different rooms / panel legs — lead confirms).
DO THE WORK: 1. Grinder on circuit 1, vacuum on circuit 2 — always.
Run cords along walls, out of walk paths, no cord across a doorway without tape/cover.
Generator: outside, exhaust away from doors/windows, then cords in.
Test: start grinder + vacuum together for 10 seconds — no trip = you're set.
DONE LOOKS LIKE: Both machines run at once without tripping. Cords tidy along walls. Nobody walks on a cord run.
SAFETY: Never run a generator indoors or in a garage — exhaust kills. No damaged cord — ever: a cut cord gets red-tagged and pulled. Keep cords dry.
COMMON MISTAKES: One circuit only (ask the lead, don't share a circuit and hope); daisy-chaining splitters.
STOP AND ASK: Breaker keeps tripping after the lead checks; generator won't start; only one working outlet in the building.
REPORT BACK: Lead: 'Power's up — grinder on one circuit, vacuum on the other, tested.'

title: Site protection — masking & tape
instructions:
Phase: Arrival & Setup | Skill level: SOLO | Status: DRAFT
WHAT IT IS: Covering and taping everything that must stay clean: floors not being coated, trim, doors, cabinets, fixtures. Coating on the wrong surface is permanent.
YOU NEED: Tape [CONSUME]; masking plastic/paper [CONSUME]; brushes for dust [APPLY]
SET UP: 1. Walk the area with the lead — he names what gets protected.
Dust off surfaces first — tape won't stick to dust.
DO THE WORK: 1. Tape edges tight and straight along everything bordering the work area.
Plastic/paper down on finished floors and fixtures, taped so it can't slide.
Cover door tracks, vents, and anything dust or flake would ruin.
DONE LOOKS LIKE: Every border is taped clean, protection is secure, no gaps at corners. Looks tidy — the client sees this first.
SAFETY: Knife/scraper care when cutting plastic/tape near finished surfaces. Ladder rules if taping high — ask before climbing anything.
COMMON MISTAKES: Taping over dust (falls off mid-coat); leaving a gap at a corner; plastic loose where someone will walk and skate on it.
STOP AND ASK: Any surface you're not sure about — tape it or ask, never guess it can get coated.
REPORT BACK: Lead: 'Protection's done' — walk it with him before coating starts.

title: Vacuum setup & bag change
instructions:
Phase: Arrival & Setup | Skill level: SOLO | Status: DRAFT
WHAT IT IS: Setting up the vacuum so it actually sucks: right vacuum, new bag, clear hose, hooked to the tool. A grinding vacuum with a full bag just blows dust around.
YOU NEED: Rigid vacuum or G22 [VAC-POWER / FLOOR]; NEW garbage bag for that vacuum [VAC-POWER]; spare bag
SET UP: 1. Take the vacuum the lead names — Rigid or G22.
Open it. Old bag OUT, new bag IN — even if the old one looks half full.
DO THE WORK: 1. Check the hose is clear (look through it / flex it) and the filter is seated.
Test suction on your hand — strong or fix it now.
Hook the hose to the grinder/tool it will serve and stage it where the work starts.
DONE LOOKS LIKE: Vacuum pulls strong, new bag in, hose hooked up, spare bag nearby.
SAFETY: Respirator ON when changing bags and emptying — concrete dust damages lungs. Bag goes straight into a garbage bag, sealed.
COMMON MISTAKES: Skipping the bag change ('looks fine'); filter left loose; hose kinked behind the machine.
STOP AND ASK: Suction weak with a new bag and clear hose — tell the lead, don't just work with a bad vacuum.
REPORT BACK: Lead: 'Vacuum's set, new bag, suction's good.'

title: Hand grinding — EDGES
instructions:
Phase: Prep — Grinding | Skill level: ASSIST+ | Status: FINAL — Aidan's steps 2026-11-02
WHAT IT IS: Grinding the edges of the floor — the strip along walls, corners, and around posts/doors where the big floor grinder cannot reach. If the edges are not ground the same as the middle, the coating will not stick there and it will peel at the walls first.
YOU NEED: DeWalt hand grinder [GRIND] — check the blade/disc before you take it; Rigid vacuum OR G22 vacuum [VAC-POWER]; new garbage bag for the vacuum + spare [VAC-POWER]; 2 extension cords [VAC-POWER]; knee pads, respirator, eye goggles, hearing protection [SAFETY]
SET UP: 1. Take the DeWalt hand grinder, the vacuum, and 2 extension cords from the trailer.
Find 2 SEPARATE circuits (two outlets on different breakers — ask the lead if you don't know how to tell). Grinder on one, vacuum on the other. Both on one circuit will trip the breaker all day.
Run the extension cords into place, along walls, out of walk paths.
Open the vacuum: take out the old garbage bag and put in a NEW one, even if the old one looks half full.
Clear/check the vacuum — hose clear, filter seated, suction strong on your hand.
Hook the vacuum hose up to the DeWalt hand grinder. No hookup = dust everywhere = you stop.
Safety gear ON before the grinder starts.
DO THE WORK: 1. Start where the lead tells you. Work in order along the wall — do not skip around.
Keep the blade FLAT on the concrete for an even grind. Tilted = grooves and an uneven edge.
Move slow and steady. Let the machine cut — do not push down hard.
Overlap each pass by half. No shiny, smooth concrete left behind — ground concrete looks dull and even.
Corners and tight spots: slow down, keep it flat, get right into the corner.
Watch the vacuum as you go. If dust starts escaping, stop — bag full, hose blocked, or hookup off. Fix it, then continue.
When your section is done, vacuum the edge you just ground, clean.
DONE LOOKS LIKE: Edge strip is dull, even, same texture as the ground floor. No shiny spots, no grooves, no dust left sitting on it. Corners done, not skipped.
SAFETY: KNEE PADS — you'll be on your knees; no pads, no grinding. RESPIRATOR on the whole time — concrete dust damages lungs. EYE GOGGLES — chips fly off the blade. NOISE PROTECTION — grinder + vacuum damage hearing over a day. Keep the cord BEHIND you, never where the blade can reach it. Let the disc stop fully before setting the grinder down.
COMMON MISTAKES: Grinder + vacuum on the same circuit (breaker trips all morning); old vacuum bag left in (no suction, dust everywhere); blade tilted (grooved edges the lead must re-do); skipping corners (coating peels at the wall first).
STOP AND ASK: Breaker keeps tripping; vacuum loses suction and a new bag doesn't fix it; blade/disc cracked or a segment missing; you hit something in the concrete you don't recognize (pipe, wire, drain).
REPORT BACK: 'Edges done from [wall] to [wall], vacuum bag changed, ready for your check.'

title: Hand grinding — WALLS / foundation
instructions:
Phase: Prep — Grinding | Skill level: ASSIST+ | Status: DRAFT — needs Aidan's wall steps (Q B3)
WHAT IT IS: Grinding the foundation walls / wall bases that get coated with the floor. Same idea as edges: the coating only sticks to ground, dull concrete — shiny wall = peeling wall.
YOU NEED: DeWalt hand grinder [GRIND]; Rigid or G22 vacuum [VAC-POWER]; new vacuum bag [VAC-POWER]; 2 extension cords [VAC-POWER]; knee pads, respirator, SEALED eye goggles, hearing protection [SAFETY]
SET UP: 1. Same power + vacuum setup as edges (B1): 2 separate circuits, new bag, vacuum hooked to the grinder.
Ask the lead how far up the wall today's job goes — grind only to that line, evenly.
DO THE WORK: 1. Blade flat against the wall, slow steady passes, overlap by half.
Work top-down so dust falls onto what you haven't finished, not onto finished wall.
Corners where wall meets floor get both cards' care — no shiny triangle left.
Vacuum as you go — wall dust drops straight down onto your ground floor.
DONE LOOKS LIKE: Wall is dull and even to the marked height, no shiny patches, wall/floor corner fully ground, fallen dust vacuumed off the floor.
SAFETY: Dust FALLS on wall work — sealed goggles, not open glasses. Respirator on the whole time. Watch your footing in the dust at the wall base. Cord behind you.
COMMON MISTAKES: Grinding past the line on one section and short on another; leaving the wall/floor corner shiny; letting wall dust sit on the prepped floor.
STOP AND ASK: Wall crumbles, cracks open up, or you find heavy pitting the lead hasn't seen — stop and show him before grinding more.
REPORT BACK: 'Walls done to the line, corner done, dust vacuumed, ready for check.'

title: Hand grinding — STAIRS / tight areas
instructions:
Phase: Prep — Grinding | Skill level: ASSIST+ | Status: DRAFT
WHAT IT IS: Hand grinding stair treads, risers, landings, and tight areas the big grinder can't reach. Stairs show every shortcut — each step gets ground fully.
YOU NEED: DeWalt hand grinder [GRIND]; vacuum + new bag [VAC-POWER]; cords [VAC-POWER]; knee pads, respirator, goggles, hearing protection [SAFETY]
SET UP: 1. Power + vacuum setup as B1 (2 circuits if available, new bag, hooked up).
Lead names the order — usually top step down, so dust falls onto unfinished steps.
DO THE WORK: 1. Grind each tread flat and fully — nose (front edge) included, it's the highest-wear spot.
Risers (the vertical face) ground the same, blade flat.
Corners where tread meets riser and wall: slow, flat, right in.
Vacuum each finished step before moving down.
DONE LOOKS LIKE: Every tread + riser dull and even, noses done, corners done, steps vacuumed clean as you descend.
SAFETY: Stairs + cords + kneeling = trip risk: cords routed behind/under control, never loose across steps you're standing on. Full PPE as B1.
COMMON MISTAKES: Skipping risers or noses; grinding treads but leaving the wall corners; dust left sitting on finished steps.
STOP AND ASK: A step is cracked, loose, or crumbling — stop and show the lead before coating plans are made on it.
REPORT BACK: 'Stairs done, top to bottom, vacuumed, ready for check.'

title: Main floor grinding — RED grinder
instructions:
Phase: Prep — Grinding | Skill level: EXPERIENCED ONLY — NEVER for temps/trainees | Status: DRAFT — boundary card
WHAT IT IS: Grinding the main floor with the big red grinder. This is a finesse machine — a bad pass pattern or wrong tooling ruins the prep for the whole job. Temps/trainees do NOT run this machine.
YOU NEED: — (lead's machine)
SET UP: Your job around it: keep the vacuum/cord support running if assigned (C1), keep the floor ahead of it clear, and stay out of its path.
DO THE WORK: NEVER assigned to temps. If the lead is on the red grinder, your work is support: vacuum, cords, tooling help when asked, debris out of the way.
DONE LOOKS LIKE: —
SAFETY: Never stand in front of a running floor grinder. Never touch tooling/diamonds on a machine that isn't stopped and unplugged.
COMMON MISTAKES: Assuming 'it's just a bigger grinder, I can try it' — you can't, and trying can end the job.
STOP AND ASK: If the machine is running wrong (noise, vibration, smell) and the operator hasn't noticed — shout and wave, don't reach for it.
REPORT BACK: 'Understood — support only' is the whole report for this card.

title: Tooling change — diamonds / PCDs
instructions:
Phase: Prep — Grinding | Skill level: ASSIST+ | Status: DRAFT
WHAT IT IS: Swapping the grinding tooling: diamonds by grit (16/30/60/80) or PCDs for coating/laitance removal, and checking every segment before the machine runs.
YOU NEED: Diamonds boxes by grit [GRIND]; PCD box [GRIND]; machine wrench/tools [GRIND]; gloves [SAFETY]
SET UP: 1. Machine STOPPED and UNPLUGGED before hands go near tooling — no exceptions.
Lead names the tooling + grit for this pass.
DO THE WORK: 1. Remove the old set, put it back in ITS labeled box — grits never mix in one box.
Fit the new set fully, every plate seated and tight.
Check EVERY segment/disc: intact, no cracks, none missing. A damaged segment does not go on the floor.
Spin-test per the lead before the pass starts.
DONE LOOKS LIKE: Full matching set fitted and tight, every segment checked, old set boxed in the right grit box.
SAFETY: Gloves for tooling (edges are sharp). Machine unplugged — treat 'just switching it off' as still live until the plug is out.
COMMON MISTAKES: Mixing grits in a box (next job's pass is ruined); one odd segment in the set; tooling left loose on the floor to get stepped on/kicked.
STOP AND ASK: Any segment cracked or missing; a plate won't seat; you're handed tooling you can't identify — ask, don't guess by looks.
REPORT BACK: 'Tooling changed to [grit/PCD], all segments checked, old set boxed.'

title: Crack chasing
instructions:
Phase: Prep — Grinding | Skill level: ASSIST+ | Status: DRAFT
WHAT IT IS: Opening up cracks with a blade/drill so filler can get IN and bond, instead of sitting on top of a hairline and popping out later.
YOU NEED: Hammer drill / chase blade setup per lead [GRIND]; vacuum [VAC-POWER]; respirator, goggles, hearing protection, knee pads [SAFETY]
SET UP: 1. Power + vacuum as B1.
Lead walks the cracks with you — which ones get chased, which ones don't.
DO THE WORK: 1. Follow the crack fully, end to end — a half-chased crack is a half-filled crack.
Steady depth per the lead — open it, don't trench it.
Vacuum the chased crack clean as you finish it — filler goes into a CLEAN crack.
DONE LOOKS LIKE: Every marked crack opened end to end and vacuumed clean, ready for D2 filling.
SAFETY: Full grinding PPE (dust is worst at the crack). Blade/drill control — both hands, cord behind you.
COMMON MISTAKES: Chasing cracks the lead didn't mark; stopping mid-crack; leaving dust packed in the chase.
STOP AND ASK: Crack keeps opening wider/deeper than expected, or you find voids under the slab sound — show the lead before filling plans change.
REPORT BACK: 'Cracks chased and vacuumed: [list areas], ready to fill.'

title: Demo / removal — old coating, tile, glue
instructions:
Phase: Prep — Grinding | Skill level: JOB-SPECIFIC — lead briefs the method | Status: DRAFT
WHAT IT IS: Removing what's on the floor now: old coating, tile, glue, paint. Method changes by job — the lead briefs today's method before anyone starts. No generic card replaces that briefing.
YOU NEED: Per the lead's briefing: PCD tooling [GRIND], scrapers [GRIND], demo tools, garbage bags [CONSUME]
SET UP: 1. Get the method briefing: machine or hand, how aggressive, what the slab underneath should look like.
Protection (A3) doubles on demo days — dust and debris go everywhere.
DO THE WORK: 1. Work to the briefed method, in sections, fully — a half-stripped section is not done.
Debris bagged as you go, not piled for later.
Watch the slab as it appears — damage, soft spots, and surprises get shown to the lead the moment you see them.
DONE LOOKS LIKE: Surface removed to the briefed standard across the whole area, debris out, slab condition reported honestly.
SAFETY: Full PPE always on demo. Extra care: hidden nails/screws in demo debris — gloves, and look before you grab.
COMMON MISTAKES: Going more aggressive than briefed and gouging the slab; burying a problem spot under debris; 'removing' by pushing material into corners.
STOP AND ASK: Slab underneath is damaged, wet, or different from what was quoted (asbestos-era tile/mastic suspicion = STOP completely and get the lead).
REPORT BACK: 'Demo done on [area], debris bagged, slab looks like: [honest description].'

title: Scraping
instructions:
Phase: Prep — Grinding | Skill level: SOLO | Status: DRAFT
WHAT IT IS: Scraping loose material, drips, glue ridges, and edges the machines left — by hand scraper. The floor gets coated exactly as it sits after scraping; anything you leave becomes part of the floor.
YOU NEED: Scrapers + spare blades [GRIND]; knee pads, gloves [SAFETY]; garbage bag [CONSUME]
SET UP: 1. Sharp blade in the scraper — a dull blade slides over ridges instead of cutting them.
Lead names the area; work it in a grid, not random wandering.
DO THE WORK: 1. Low angle, firm strokes, cut ridges and loose bits off flush.
Hand-check as you go — your palm finds what your eyes miss.
Sweep/vacuum your scrapings out of the area before moving on.
DONE LOOKS LIKE: Area is flat to a hand-check, no ridges or loose flakes, scrapings gone.
SAFETY: Blade care: cut away from your body, spare blades handled by the edges. Knee pads — scraping is kneeling work.
COMMON MISTAKES: Wandering (missed patches everywhere); dull blade all day; scrapings left to get vacuumed 'later' into the coating prep.
STOP AND ASK: Anything that won't scrape because it's bonded INTO a defect — show the lead, it may need grinding or patching, not force.
REPORT BACK: '[Area] scraped and hand-checked, scrapings out.'

title: Vacuuming — EDGES (vacuum man)
instructions:
Phase: Cleaning | Skill level: SOLO | Status: DRAFT
WHAT IT IS: You ARE the dust control while hand grinding runs: your vacuum rides with the grinder so dust never gets airborne or settles back on prepped floor.
YOU NEED: The grinder's vacuum — Rigid or G22 [VAC-POWER]; spare bags [VAC-POWER]; respirator [SAFETY]
SET UP: 1. You set the vacuum up first (A4): new bag, strong suction, hose ready.
Pair with your grinder man before he starts — you move when he moves.
DO THE WORK: 1. Keep the hose hooked to his grinder and untangled — manage his cord + hose so he never stops for them.
When he pauses, vacuum the ground edge clean immediately.
Watch your suction: dust escaping = bag/hose/hookup problem — fix it on the spot (that's your main job).
Empty/check the bag at every break, not when it's already choking.
DONE LOOKS LIKE: No dust plume while grinding runs, edges clean behind the grinder, grinder man never waits on you.
SAFETY: Respirator on whenever grinding is running near you. Bag changes as A4 — bag sealed straight into garbage.
COMMON MISTAKES: Wandering off while grinding continues; letting the hose kink/pull off; bag so full the vacuum whines — change it before that.
STOP AND ASK: Vacuum dies, loses suction for good, or the grinder man is outpacing what one vacuum can hold — tell the lead early.
REPORT BACK: 'Vacuum kept up, bag changed [x] times, edges clean behind the grinder.'

title: Full floor vacuum — HEPA pass before coating
instructions:
Phase: Cleaning | Skill level: SOLO — gate-checked | Status: DRAFT
WHAT IT IS: The last clean before any coating touches the floor. Whatever dust is on that floor when coating starts is IN the floor forever. This vacuum is slow, complete, and checked.
YOU NEED: Large vacuum / HEPA vacuum [FLOOR / VAC-POWER]; NEW bag [VAC-POWER]; hand brush [APPLY]; respirator [SAFETY]
SET UP: 1. NEW bag in — a coating vacuum never starts on yesterday's bag.
Floor must be fully prepped and scraped first — if prep isn't finished, this isn't your start signal; ask the lead.
DO THE WORK: 1. Work the floor in lanes, overlapping, wall to wall — pattern, not wandering.
Edges and corners TWICE — dust hides there.
Slow down: this pass is about pickup, not speed.
After lanes: brush + vacuum door tracks, ledges, and anywhere dust settled.
Hand-check / light-check per the lead before you call it done.
DONE LOOKS LIKE: Whole floor lane-vacuumed, edges double-done, no visible dust anywhere, ready for the lead's prep gate check (F3).
SAFETY: Respirator on — you're stirring the finest dust of the day. Empty the bag outside the prepped area, sealed.
COMMON MISTAKES: Rushing lanes; edges once; vacuuming BEFORE patching/scraping is actually done (you'll do it twice and trust it less).
STOP AND ASK: You find dust you cannot remove (damp patches, dust bleeding from cracks) — stop before coating, show the lead.
REPORT BACK: 'Floor vacuumed wall to wall, edges twice, ready for the gate check.'

title: Dust & wipe-down
instructions:
Phase: Cleaning | Skill level: SOLO | Status: DRAFT
WHAT IT IS: Wiping dust off walls, ledges, tops of fixtures, and door tracks near the work area so it can't fall or blow into wet coating later.
YOU NEED: Wipes [CONSUME]; rags [CONSUME]; small vacuum or brush [APPLY]
SET UP: 1. Do this AFTER grinding in the area stops and BEFORE coating starts — order matters.
Top-down: highest surfaces first.
DO THE WORK: 1. Wipe ledges, wall tops, window sills, door tracks, fixture tops bordering the floor.
Anything you knock loose falls to the floor — C2 vacuum comes after you if it's a coat day; confirm order with the lead.
DONE LOOKS LIKE: Bordering surfaces dust-free to a hand-wipe check (rag comes away clean).
SAFETY: Respirator if dust is still airborne. No wet wipes on surfaces near a floor about to be coated unless the lead says so — moisture is the enemy.
COMMON MISTAKES: Wiping after the floor's final vacuum (dust rains onto a clean floor); dry-wiping in circles that just move dust around.
STOP AND ASK: Dust keeps coming from somewhere (vent, open door draft) — tell the lead before coating, not during.
REPORT BACK: 'Wipe-down done, rag checks clean.'

title: Garbage & debris — all day
instructions:
Phase: Cleaning | Skill level: SOLO | Status: DRAFT
WHAT IT IS: Keeping the site clean WHILE work runs: bags, demo debris, used consumables. A clean site is faster, safer, and it's what the client judges at 4 PM.
YOU NEED: Garbage bags [CONSUME]; gloves [SAFETY]
SET UP: 1. One garbage bag staged open near the work, one spare. Full bag never sits — it's tied and out.
DO THE WORK: 1. Collect as you go: tape backs, wipe waste, scrapings, demo bits.
Full bags to the agreed spot (trailer/dumpster per lead) — never piled by the client's door.
End of each phase: walk your area, leave it clean for the next phase.
DONE LOOKS LIKE: No loose debris anywhere in the work area at any check; bags staged and moving out all day.
SAFETY: Gloves for debris (hidden sharp edges/nails). Lift bags with legs — demo bags are heavy.
COMMON MISTAKES: One giant pile 'for later'; bags left in the client's walkway/driveway show-zone; sharp debris loose in a thin bag waiting to tear.
STOP AND ASK: You find something that isn't HARDBOND garbage (client property in the work zone, hazardous-looking material) — hand it to the lead, don't bin it.
REPORT BACK: 'Site's clean, [x] bags out.'

title: Patching — holes, pitting, divots
instructions:
Phase: Repairs | Skill level: ASSIST+ | Status: DRAFT
WHAT IT IS: Filling holes, pitting, and damaged areas so the finished floor is flat and the coating isn't bridging holes. RULE OF THE TRADE HERE: prep is 100% before the next step — skipped patching has forced FULL RECOATS on this crew.
YOU NEED: Patch material [REPAIR]; trowels [APPLY]; scraper [GRIND]; vacuum [VAC-POWER]; gloves, knee pads [SAFETY]
SET UP: 1. Area ground + vacuumed FIRST — patch goes on clean, prepped concrete only.
Lead names the product + consistency for today; watch his first patch before you mix/fetch.
DO THE WORK: 1. Work patch into the hole/pit fully — no air pocket under a skin of material.
Strike it flat/flush with the surrounding floor — a patch hump is tomorrow's bump under coating.
Do the area COMPLETELY: walk it, hand-check, mark missed pits, do them now.
Per product: respect the cure before grinding/sanding it flush (lead calls timing).
DONE LOOKS LIKE: Every hole/pit in the area filled flush, no skins over voids, area ready for flush-grind/vacuum.
SAFETY: Gloves with patch resins — skin contact sensitizes over time; wash at breaks. Knee pads — patching is floor-level work.
COMMON MISTAKES: Skipping 'small' pitting (it telegraphs through coating); patching over dust; humps left because 'the coating will hide it' — it won't.
STOP AND ASK: Pitting far worse than quoted once you start, or a hole that keeps swallowing material (void) — show the lead.
REPORT BACK: 'Patching done on [area], all of it, ready for flush check.'

title: Crack filling
instructions:
Phase: Repairs | Skill level: ASSIST+ | Status: DRAFT
WHAT IT IS: Filling chased cracks flush so they don't telegraph through the finished floor or reopen as lines in the coating.
YOU NEED: Crack filler [REPAIR]; trowel/scraper [APPLY]; vacuum [VAC-POWER]; gloves, knee pads [SAFETY]
SET UP: 1. Cracks must be chased (B6) and vacuumed clean first — filler into dust is filler on dust.
Lead names the filler + working method today.
DO THE WORK: 1. Fill the full length, working material INTO the chase, not across the top.
Strike flush — excess smeared wide becomes a visible band.
Re-check after it sets per the lead: any sink-back gets a second pass now, not after coating.
DONE LOOKS LIKE: Every chased crack filled flush its whole length, no smear bands, no sink gaps.
SAFETY: Gloves (resin fillers). Knee pads.
COMMON MISTAKES: Bridging the top of the chase; wide smears; calling it done before the set/re-check.
STOP AND ASK: Crack moves/creaks underfoot or filler won't set — lead sees it before coating.
REPORT BACK: 'Cracks filled: [areas], re-checked after set.'

title: Detail repair — edges, drains, posts
instructions:
Phase: Repairs | Skill level: ASSIST+ | Status: DRAFT
WHAT IT IS: The small repairs machines and big trowels miss: around drains, posts, door frames, and corners. Details are where a floor looks cheap or looks pro.
YOU NEED: Patch/filler per lead [REPAIR]; small trowels + brushes [APPLY]; tape [CONSUME]; gloves, knee pads [SAFETY]
SET UP: 1. Lead walks the details with you and names each one — details are assigned, not discovered mid-coat.
Tape-protect drains/fixtures that must stay clean (A3 method).
DO THE WORK: 1. One detail at a time, finished fully before the next.
Keep repair material off finished/protected surfaces — wipe slips immediately per lead.
Match the surrounding prep — a smooth patch in a ground field shows.
DONE LOOKS LIKE: Every named detail repaired flush and clean, protection intact, nothing smeared.
SAFETY: Gloves; knee pads. Care with blades/tape near fixtures.
COMMON MISTAKES: Rushing details because they're small; leaving one 'for later' that the coat then reaches first.
STOP AND ASK: A detail is worse inside than it looked (rotted frame, moving drain) — lead decides, you don't bury it.
REPORT BACK: 'Details done: [list], ready for check.'

title: Mixing station
instructions:
Phase: Coating | Skill level: ASSIST+ | Status: DRAFT
WHAT IT IS: Running the mix: measuring, mixing, and timing kits so the floor crew never waits and no kit dies in the bucket. Pot life is a clock — some of our resins give you 10–12 minutes, not 'whenever'.
YOU NEED: Mixing drill + paddles [MIX]; buckets [MIX]; measuring containers [MIX]; pot-life TIMER [MIX]; gloves + goggles [SAFETY]; the job's kits staged by the lead [COAT]
SET UP: 1. Kits staged by system — you mix ONLY what the lead calls, in the order he calls it.
Timer at the station, visible. Bucket + paddle clean before the first mix.
DO THE WORK: 1. Measure EXACTLY per the product's ratio (lead states it for today's product) — never eyeball, never split a kit where the product demands full units.
Mix fully: sides, bottom, corners — unmixed material in a corner ruins a section.
START THE TIMER the moment parts combine. Call the time out.
Deliver the kit to the floor immediately and say its age ('mixed 2 minutes ago').
Bucket/paddle cleaned or swapped before the next mix — old resin contaminates new.
DONE LOOKS LIKE: Every kit mixed exact, timed, and on the floor fresh; floor crew never stands waiting; no kit lost to pot life at the station.
SAFETY: GOGGLES + GLOVES for mixing — resin in eyes/skin is the station's real hazard. Respirator if the lead calls it for the product/space.
COMMON MISTAKES: Eyeballing ratios; 'one quick extra section' from a dying kit; unmixed corners; timer forgotten on a fast product (PE-VRM pot life is 10–12 min).
STOP AND ASK: Anything unclear about ratio/product/order — ASK BEFORE YOU MIX. A mixed wrong kit is garbage and everyone's time.
REPORT BACK: 'Kit [n] mixed at [time], on the floor at [age].' — every kit, out loud.

title: Material runner
instructions:
Phase: Coating | Skill level: SOLO | Status: DRAFT
WHAT IT IS: Keeping the coating crew fed: kits, flake boxes, rollers, buckets — at their elbows before they ask. Coating can't pause; a starved squeegee man is a ruined section.
YOU NEED: Whatever the phase needs: kits [COAT]; flake boxes [FLAKE]; rollers [APPLY]; buckets [MIX]; spike shoes if swapping [APPLY]
SET UP: 1. Before the coat starts: stage the phase's materials at the edge of the work, in USE ORDER.
Know the next thing they'll need before they need it — watch the work, not your phone.
DO THE WORK: 1. Deliver to the edge — NEVER walk onto wet coating except in spike shoes when told.
Open/stage the next kit or flake box ahead of the need.
Take empties AWAY — the work edge stays clear.
Call out what you're bringing ('next flake box in 2 minutes') so nobody wonders.
DONE LOOKS LIKE: Coating crew never stops for material; work edge clear of empties; next item always staged.
SAFETY: Spike shoes ONLY when told and only on wet coating — spikes on finished/dry areas or client floors destroy surfaces. Kits are heavy — lift properly, two hands.
COMMON MISTAKES: Watching instead of anticipating; stepping onto wet floor in boots (ends jobs); staging everything at once into a clutter pile.
STOP AND ASK: Stock runs short mid-coat (kits/flake won't finish the area) — tell the lead THE MOMENT you see it, not when the last box opens.
REPORT BACK: 'You're set — next [item] staged, [x] kits left after this one.'

title: Basecoat — squeegee
instructions:
Phase: Coating | Skill level: EXPERIENCED ONLY | Status: DRAFT — boundary card
WHAT IT IS: Spreading the basecoat at the right film thickness with the squeegee. Coverage is spec'd (a kit covers what it covers) — spreading thin to 'make it stretch' breaks the product's rating and the floor. Experienced men only.
YOU NEED: — (lead's tools)
SET UP: Your job around it: mixing station (E1) or runner (E2) if assigned — the squeegee man must never leave the floor to fetch.
DO THE WORK: NEVER assigned to temps/trainees. Support roles only, done exactly as briefed.
DONE LOOKS LIKE: —
SAFETY: Never step on wet coating without spike shoes + the lead's say-so.
COMMON MISTAKES: Offering to 'just spread a bit' — untrained spreading is how film thickness dies.
STOP AND ASK: Kit count won't cover the area at spec — if you notice it on the station/runner, say it immediately.
REPORT BACK: 'Support only — station/runner covered' is your report.

title: Cross roll — 18in squeegee
instructions:
Phase: Coating | Skill level: NEVER for temps/trainees — finesse task | Status: DRAFT — boundary card
WHAT IT IS: The cross-roll pass that evens the coat. It takes finesse to get 100% right — too much or too little pressure leaves lines in the finished floor. Named off-limits (this includes Shahmir until cleared).
YOU NEED: — (lead's tools)
SET UP: Your job: keep material coming (E2), watch edges/lighting if asked, stay off the coat.
DO THE WORK: NEVER assigned to temps/trainees. No exceptions because the day is busy.
DONE LOOKS LIKE: —
SAFETY: Stay off wet coating without spikes + lead instruction.
COMMON MISTAKES: Grabbing the squeegee during a break 'to help' — a 'helpful' pass can line a whole section.
STOP AND ASK: If you see a miss/line the roller hasn't reached yet — point it out to the LEAD, don't fix it yourself.
REPORT BACK: 'Understood — off the roll, support only.'

title: Coating edges & walls — cutting in
instructions:
Phase: Coating | Skill level: ASSIST+ | Status: DRAFT
WHAT IT IS: Brushing/rolling the coating onto edges, wall bases, and details the squeegee can't reach, keeping pace just ahead of/alongside the main coat so wet edges meet wet edges.
YOU NEED: Chip brushes + small rollers [APPLY]; the phase's mixed material (from E1 station); tape check from A3; gloves [SAFETY]; spike shoes if told [APPLY]
SET UP: 1. Protection/tape checked before material arrives — you can't tape into wet coating.
Work the section the lead names, in his order — edge work out of sequence strands a wet edge.
DO THE WORK: 1. Load, lay, and even the material to match the field coat — no ridges at your line, no starved edges.
Keep a wet edge: your section must meet the main coat while both are wet.
Material on tape/trim/fixtures gets cleaned the second it happens, per the lead.
DONE LOOKS LIKE: Edges + walls coated evenly, meeting the field wet, no misses at corners, nothing on protected surfaces.
SAFETY: Gloves — you'll be closest to the resin all day. Kneeling pads when working low edges.
COMMON MISTAKES: Falling behind the main coat (dry seam line); ridges left at the squeegee line; 'catching up' by slopping extra on corners.
STOP AND ASK: Main coat is gaining on you and you can't hold the wet edge — call it early so the lead rebalances crew.
REPORT BACK: 'Edges/walls done to [point], wet edge held.'

title: Flake broadcast
instructions:
Phase: Coating | Skill level: ASSIST+ | Status: DRAFT
WHAT IT IS: Throwing decorative flake into the wet basecoat to FULL coverage (broadcast to rejection): the floor should look like flake, not like coating with sprinkles — where the job spec calls full broadcast.
YOU NEED: Flake boxes for today's colour [FLAKE]; broadcast bucket [FLAKE]; spike shoes [APPLY]; gloves [SAFETY]
SET UP: 1. Boxes staged at the work edge in order (E2 keeps you fed).
Spike shoes ON before you step onto wet coat — and you enter/exit where the lead says.
DO THE WORK: 1. Handfuls tossed UP so flake rains down evenly — never thrown forward in clumps.
Work backwards across your section, keeping the wet edge covered as it advances.
Full coverage: no wet coating showing through when you finish a section. Walk the light — thin spots show at an angle.
Broadcast rate matters: follow the lead's call for this job (full rejection vs partial % — e.g. some jobs run 10–30% accent blends).
DONE LOOKS LIKE: Section fully covered to the called rate, even — no clumps, no thin windows, no footprints in bare coat.
SAFETY: Spike shoes on wet coat only, and shuffled — lifting a spiked foot straight through thin coat tears it. Gloves optional but flake dust dries skin.
COMMON MISTAKES: Clumping from throwing forward; thin spots at the far edge of a section; running low and quietly stretching flake — NEVER stretch; call the shortage.
STOP AND ASK: Flake won't finish the area, colour/box looks wrong vs the job, or you step wrong and mark the coat — lead hears it immediately.
REPORT BACK: 'Broadcast done to [point], coverage full, [x] boxes left.'

title: Flake scrape & reclaim
instructions:
Phase: Coating | Skill level: SOLO after training | Status: DRAFT
WHAT IT IS: After the flake coat cures: scraping down the loose/high flake and vacuuming so the surface is flat and ready for topcoat. What you scrape loose gets vacuumed — clean reclaim may be saved per the lead.
YOU NEED: Scrapers [GRIND]; vacuum + fresh bag [VAC-POWER]; buckets for reclaim [FLAKE]; knee pads, respirator [SAFETY]
SET UP: 1. ONLY when the lead confirms the coat is cured enough — scraping early tears the floor.
Fresh vacuum bag — this pass loads a vacuum fast.
DO THE WORK: 1. Scrape flat passes across the whole area — knock down high flake, don't gouge.
Vacuum the whole area thoroughly — loose flake left behind ends up in the topcoat.
Reclaim: save only what the lead says is clean enough; contaminated flake is garbage, no debate at the bucket.
DONE LOOKS LIKE: Surface evenly scraped, fully vacuumed, no loose flake anywhere, ready for topcoat inspection.
SAFETY: Respirator — scraped flake + dust. Knee pads.
COMMON MISTAKES: Scraping before the cure call; saving dirty reclaim to 'help the count'; a quick vacuum that leaves drifts in corners.
STOP AND ASK: Flake comes UP in sheets or the coat feels soft anywhere — stop, lead checks cure before anyone else scrapes it.
REPORT BACK: 'Scraped + vacuumed, reclaim: [saved/garbage], ready for topcoat check.'

title: Topcoat application
instructions:
Phase: Coating | Skill level: EXPERIENCED ONLY | Status: DRAFT — boundary card
WHAT IT IS: The final clear coat that seals the floor. It's the surface the client sees and touches — misses, lines, and contamination all show forever. Experienced men only.
YOU NEED: — (lead's tools)
SET UP: Your job around it: runner (E2), lighting/watch support if assigned as E9, and keeping EVERYTHING (dust, people, pets, doors) away from the wet floor.
DO THE WORK: NEVER assigned to temps/trainees. Support roles only.
DONE LOOKS LIKE: Finished topcoat must stay untouched: foot traffic 1 day, cars/heavy 2 days — you are part of enforcing that at the door.
SAFETY: Opening a door/window 'for air' on your own — dust and bugs land in wet topcoat. Ventilation changes are the lead's call only.
COMMON MISTAKES: Anything falls/blows into the wet topcoat, or someone is about to walk on it — you stop it / report it instantly.
STOP AND ASK: 'Support covered — floor guarded.'
REPORT BACK:

title: Topcoat support — spikes, light, watch
instructions:
Phase: Coating | Skill level: ASSIST+ | Status: DRAFT
WHAT IT IS: Supporting the topcoat pass: holding light at the right angle, watching for misses and debris, and moving in spikes only where told. Topcoat misses hide at straight-on views and show at an angle — you're the angle.
YOU NEED: Work light [VAC-POWER]; spike shoes [APPLY]; lint-free wipe per lead [CONSUME]
SET UP: 1. Light positioned per the applicator — low angle across the surface.
Know the pass pattern before it starts so your light stays ahead of it.
DO THE WORK: 1. Track the applicator: light angled, call misses ('holiday at the post') the moment you see them.
Watch for hairs, bugs, dust nibs — point, don't touch, unless the lead hands you the fix.
In spikes: shuffle, minimal steps, exit on the called path.
DONE LOOKS LIKE: No missed patches in the finished light-check; applicator never waits for light; no stray prints in or out.
SAFETY: Spikes discipline as E6/E8. Never lean over wet coat with loose clothing/tools dangling.
COMMON MISTAKES: Chasing a miss into the middle yourself; light straight-on (hides everything); stepping out the wrong path.
STOP AND ASK: A defect you can't classify, or contamination spreading (fisheyes) — lead hears it on the first patch, not the tenth.
REPORT BACK: 'Watch kept — misses called: [none/list], floor clear.'

title: Conditions readings
instructions:
Phase: Conditions & QC | Skill level: ASSIST+ — trained only | Status: DRAFT
WHAT IT IS: Reading and recording the slab's conditions: air temp, slab temp (IR gun), humidity, moisture. Coating decisions are product-specific — these numbers decide GO / heat / hold, and they're written down, never remembered.
YOU NEED: IR slab thermometer [TEST]; moisture meter [TEST]; humidity/air reader [TEST]; hardness tester if called [TEST]; the Daily Sheet / job notes to write into
SET UP: 1. Take the TEST grab-box — it goes in first and out first for a reason.
Lead names when readings happen (arrival, pre-coat at the day's actual peak, etc.).
DO THE WORK: 1. Slab IR: readings across the area (corners + middle + the coldest spot you can find) — one warm reading in the sun is not the slab.
Air temp + humidity at floor level in the space.
Moisture per the meter + lead's method where the job calls for a test.
WRITE IT DOWN with the time, immediately: air / slab IR (low reading) / humidity / moisture.
DONE LOOKS LIKE: A written, timed set of readings the lead can make the call from — worst-spot numbers included, not just averages.
SAFETY: No safety items beyond site standard. Careful with meter pins/points.
COMMON MISTAKES: One reading in the warmest spot; numbers 'remembered' until lunch; rounding a 6 into a 7 — the floor doesn't care about your optimism.
STOP AND ASK: A reading looks wrong vs the space (meter acting up, slab wet somewhere unexpected) — retake once, then show the lead.
REPORT BACK: 'Readings at [time]: air [x], slab low [x], humidity [x]%, moisture [x] — written down.'

title: Photos — before / during / after
instructions:
Phase: Conditions & QC | Skill level: SOLO | Status: DRAFT
WHAT IT IS: Shooting the job record: same angles before, during, and after. Photos settle 'was that crack already there' and prove the prep nobody sees under a finished floor.
YOU NEED: Phone/camera; the job's photo list if the lead names specific shots
SET UP: 1. BEFORE anything moves: walk the job and shoot every wall/section + close-ups of existing damage, cracks, stains.
DO THE WORK: 1. Same angles at each phase the lead calls (post-grind prep is the money shot — it disappears under coating).
Close-ups: defects before repair, repairs after, conditions meter readings if asked.
AFTER: finished floor, same angles as the befores, good light.
DONE LOOKS LIKE: A matched before/during/after set exists for the job, defects documented, nothing key left unshot.
SAFETY: Client privacy: shoot the WORK — no people, no family photos/valuables in frame if avoidable. Photos of a client's home stay work-only.
COMMON MISTAKES: Only pretty afters (useless in a dispute); prep phase skipped; shooting from different angles so pairs don't compare.
STOP AND ASK: Existing damage worse than expected (it needs documenting + lead's eyes BEFORE work covers it).
REPORT BACK: 'Photos done: before [x], prep [x], after pending/done.'

title: Prep gate check — 100% before next phase
instructions:
Phase: Conditions & QC | Skill level: LEAD ONLY | Status: DRAFT — boundary card
WHAT IT IS: The walk that decides whether the next phase starts. HARDBOND rule: prep is 100% before the next step — no exceptions for the clock. Skipped patching/prep has forced full recoats.
YOU NEED: — (lead's check)
SET UP: Your job: your areas presented honestly — done means done, and the thing you're unsure about gets pointed at, not hidden.
DO THE WORK: LEAD ONLY. Nobody starts the next phase on their own call, ever. If the lead hasn't cleared it, it isn't cleared.
DONE LOOKS LIKE: All crew can go home knowing the floor was right.
SAFETY: —
COMMON MISTAKES: Starting to 'get ahead' on the next phase before the gate — you're not ahead, you're redoing it.
STOP AND ASK: You already know a spot will fail the gate — say it before he finds it. That honesty is the job.
REPORT BACK: '[Area] ready for your gate check — and watch [spot], I'm not sure about it.'

title: Site cleanup
instructions:
Phase: Closeout | Skill level: SOLO | Status: DRAFT
WHAT IT IS: Leaving the client's space clean: floors swept, debris out, their stuff respected. The last thing the client sees is how you left — it decides the review more than the middle of the job.
YOU NEED: Brooms/dustpan, garbage bags [CONSUME]; vacuum for a finish pass if called [VAC-POWER]
SET UP: 1. Cleanup starts when the lead calls closeout — not while coating decisions are still live.
DO THE WORK: 1. Work area + paths + driveway/trailer zone: swept and clear.
Client's items back where they were if anything was moved (per lead).
All garbage OUT to the agreed spot/trailer — nothing left 'for the client to toss'.
DONE LOOKS LIKE: Site visibly cleaner than mid-job tidy: no debris, no bags, no gear marks, paths clear.
SAFETY: Gloves for debris. Care moving gear past finished surfaces — a scuffed wall at 5 PM is still a scuffed wall.
COMMON MISTAKES: Sweeping dust INTO the finished floor's edge; leaving tape backs and wipe waste in corners.
STOP AND ASK: You find damage — yours, or pre-existing you can't prove — show the lead before leaving, with photos if F2 applies.
REPORT BACK: 'Site cleaned, garbage out, paths clear.'

title: Trailer reload — by zone & code
instructions:
Phase: Closeout | Skill level: SOLO — checked | Status: DRAFT
WHAT IT IS: Loading the trailer back the way the Trailer Map says: every item in its labeled box, box in its coded spot. Tomorrow's load time is decided by tonight's reload.
YOU NEED: Trailer Map tab (zones/codes); Return Checklist (Trailer Checks tab); red tags for low/empty items
SET UP: 1. Reload to the Map + Return Checklist — not to 'where it fit'.
DO THE WORK: 1. Partial kits marked BEFORE they go on the shelf: product / date / job / amount left — on the lid.
Dirty tools separated — nothing dirty back on a clean shelf.
Vacuum bags checked; full out, new staged. Cords coiled the standard way; damaged cord red-tagged OUT.
Last-one-taken items get a RED TAG — that's tomorrow's buy list.
Heavy low, resins upright in the tray, floor spots back to their tape marks.
DONE LOOKS LIKE: Trailer looks like the shelf photos in the Trailer Map tab. Doors close on order, not on a pile.
SAFETY: Two-person lifts for the red grinder/heavy kits on ramps. Watch footing — end of day is when injuries happen.
COMMON MISTAKES: 'Mostly back'; partials unmarked (tomorrow they're mystery kits); red tags skipped because you're tired — the tag IS the job.
STOP AND ASK: Anything missing, broken, or borrowed-not-returned — it goes on the Return Checklist + to the lead tonight, not discovered next job.
REPORT BACK: 'Reload done to the map. Red tags: [list or none]. Missing/broken: [list or none].'

title: Tape off & cure signage
instructions:
Phase: Closeout | Skill level: SOLO | Status: DRAFT
WHAT IT IS: Closing the finished floor properly: taped off so nobody walks it, and the cure rules left where the client will see them — foot traffic 1 day, cars/heavy traffic 2 days.
YOU NEED: Tape [CONSUME]; cure note/signage per lead
SET UP: 1. Only after the final coat is down and the lead confirms the floor is in cure.
DO THE WORK: 1. Tape across every entry to the floor — doorways, stairs, garage doors — no polite gap someone will 'just step through'.
Cure note placed as the lead directs (door/client handoff): 1 day before foot traffic, 2 days before cars/heavy items.
Check exterior doors/garage door are secured as the lead directs.
DONE LOOKS LIKE: Every entry taped, cure note in place, no path onto the floor left open.
SAFETY: Never step onto the curing floor to place tape — work from the edges/thresholds.
COMMON MISTAKES: One entry left untaped ('nobody uses that door' — somebody does); cure times told from memory wrongly — the note says 1 day feet / 2 days cars.
STOP AND ASK: An entry that can't be taped (traffic must pass) — lead decides the barrier, you don't improvise one.
REPORT BACK: 'Taped off, cure note left: 1 day feet, 2 days cars.'

title: End-of-day report
instructions:
Phase: Closeout | Skill level: EVERYONE — every day | Status: DRAFT
WHAT IT IS: Your 60-second report to the lead before you leave: what you finished, what you didn't, what broke or ran out. Surprises belong at 5 PM today, not at 8 AM tomorrow on the next job.
YOU NEED: —
SET UP: 1. Think it through before the lead asks: DONE / NOT DONE / PROBLEMS / BROKEN-LOW, for YOUR assignments.
DO THE WORK: 1. Report in that order, honestly — 'not done' with a reason beats 'done' that isn't.
Broken/low/missing goes in the same breath — it feeds the buy list and tomorrow's load.
If your check-offs are in the Crew Picker, mark Done / Not done / Partial there as the lead directs.
DONE LOOKS LIKE: Lead knows the true state of every assignment you held, and the trailer/buy list reflect it.
SAFETY: —
COMMON MISTAKES: Reporting the day you wish you'd had; assuming someone else mentioned the broken/low item.
STOP AND ASK: Anything you know will bite tomorrow (cure worry, low stock, a defect you covered) — tonight is when it gets said. Always.
REPORT BACK: 'My report: done [x], not done [y + why], broken/low [z].'
